articles.text: General Grant is much better. He is now resting quietly at Mt. McGregor and in every way his condition is improving.
articles.summary: General Grant reported much better and resting at Mt. McGregor.

articles.text: Beginning with July 1, the reduced rate on postage will go into effect. Instead of being two cents per half ounce it will be two cents per ounce.
articles.summary: The reduced postage rate of two cents per ounce takes effect July 1.

articles.text: Poor Keily, he of anti-Catholic fame is having a parrot and monkey time getting a government appointment. He was first given a ministerial position to Italy, the poorest place in the world to send him and on account of his pronounced anti-Catholic sentiments the Italian government very properly refused to receive him. Lately he was appointed minister to Austria and now the Austrian government refuses to receive him.
articles.summary: Editorial on A. M. Keiley's rejection as U.S. minister by Italy and then Austria.

articles.text: President Cleveland is in earnest about enforcing the executive order for the vacation of the Winnebago and Crow Creek reservations. We have already expressed our opinion of the injustice of this last order as it will bankrupt many bona fide settlers who were induced to settle there when the reservation was opened by the order of President Arthur. We have seen no reason to change our opinion and now as before consider the order for the settlers to move as a mere catch-penny devise of the administration to obtain the support of th maudlin Indian sympathizers of the east.
articles.summary: Editorial condemning Cleveland's order removing settlers from the Winnebago and Crow Creek reservations.

articles.text: From late and authentic sources we learn that a New York company has been organized, the capital subscribed and nearly all preliminary arrangements made toward building the railroad from the Hay Creek coal mines along the Belle Fourche and into Lead City. All the iron will be shipped to Medora and freighted from here. This will bring Deadwood within a hundred and sixty miles wagon road from Medora. The project of building a railroad from Medora to intersect this road at De Mores, on the Belle Fourche, is by no means a dead one and in fact depends in a great measure upon the completion of the Hay Creek coal road.
articles.summary: A New York company has been organized to build a railroad from the Hay Creek coal mines to Lead City, with iron to be freighted from Medora.

articles.text: Stark Co's. assessor has completed his work of assessing Billings county and now the question is whether it will be cheaper to pay all the taxes to another county which does not possess as much taxable property as Billings or to run our own county organization. The rate will tell the story. If we are taxed over $2,000 it will pay pecuniarily to organize, not taking into consideration the dependent position we are now in and the fact of having to transact all our legal business in Mandan and Dickinson. It will cost about $6,000 or $7,000 a year to organize and the railroad will yield about $4,000 in taxes. Whether under these circumstances it will pay to organize is a business proposition to be settled by our citizens.
articles.summary: Stark County's assessor has assessed Billings County; the paper weighs whether Billings should organize its own county government.

articles.text: The government has sent a special agent to the Crow reservation to enquire into their condition. The Dawes party will also come up through Wyoming and probably go as far north as the southern limit of the Crow reservation. These visits are doubtless due to the petition of the Montana stockgrowers, association requesting the government to examine into the condition of the Indians. We hope that some definite action will be taken at the next session of Congress and that in all justice to both intending settlers and Indians, the government will throw open a part at least of the reservation, now entirely unused by the Indians and see that they are properly compensated, most desirable things to all concerned.
articles.summary: A government agent and the Dawes party will visit the Crow reservation; the paper urges opening part of it to settlement.

articles.text: Politics in England are in an extremely muddled state. It is very possible that Gladstone voluntarily had himself and party defeated so as to put the burden of running the government upon the Conservatives. Lord Salisbury, as leader of this party is placed in the unenviable situation of occupying the position of Premier and making almost a certain failure on account of the presant chaotic condition of England's foreign and Irish policy or giving up the power again to Gladstone and the Liberals. This will show want of back bone on Salisbury's part and he is equally allured and repelled by his own chances of failure or success Meanwhile Victoria is coquetting with both parties and compelling the leaders to follow her all over the Highlands to obtain an interview.
articles.summary: Editorial on the British cabinet crisis between Gladstone and Salisbury.

articles.text: Gen. Brisbin in a recent communication to the National cattle and horse growers' association gives a number of able reasons why the eradication of pleuro-pneumonia should be placed in the hands of the government. Among the reasons are the following: The government can make it uniform in all the states at the same time; it can best stand the expense; it can best determine the extent, location and prevalence of the disease; it will adopt one system of extirpation; it should take the matter in hand because the disease threatens to become a national calamity; the disease is now only prevalent in the fenced or eastern regions and prompt measures will guarantee that it will never appear in the unfenced regions of the west where its eradication will prove well-nigh impossible. The Cow Boy the more readily coincides with Gen. Brisbin, as his argument is directly in line with what we have so often advocated. We wish to go further, however, and put the eradication of every contagious diease in the hands of the general government. In this way only can contagious diseases be successfully stamped out. This will also put an end to the jealousy and hatred arising beween different states and territories on account of the quarantine laws. The placing of contagious diseases in the hands of the government is a question calling for the earnest consideration of all stock associations.
articles.summary: The paper endorses Gen. Brisbin's call for federal control of pleuro-pneumonia eradication and goes further to urge federal control of all contagious stock diseases.

articles.headline: Annoncement.
articles.text:
Cattle-men of the Little Missouri river are advised that the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Company, will give them during June for the beef and dry cows that they wish to sell, Chicago prices less seventy cents per hundred to cover freight and shrinkage. The cattle to be delivered in the evening at the Sully Creek corrals and weighed in the morning.

Marquis de Mores,
President.
articles.summary: The Marquis de Mores announces the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Co. will buy beef and dry cows in June at Chicago prices less seventy cents per hundred, delivered at the Sully Creek corrals.

articles.text:
From Custer Trail Ranch about April 1st., a red or strawberry roan pony seven or eight years old, branded J on right shoulder and thigh, HT connected (Tarbell's brand) with 7 under on left shoulder and flying V on left thigh. Had on Ortmayer and Son's, of Chicago, saddle, bridle and hackamore.

Custer Trail Cattle Co.
F. Alden Eaton, Supt.

Word may also be sent to the Cow Boy office.
articles.summary: Custer Trail Cattle Co. notice of a roan pony with saddle strayed from the ranch about April 1.

articles.text: The splendid growth of grass has had the effect of making the round-ups this year shorter than ever before, in spite of the increased number of cattle.
articles.summary: Abundant grass made this year's round-ups shorter than ever.

articles.text: From reliable sources we learn that the cattle loss in the Black Hills country was at least ten per cent. This is accounted for by the deep and lasting snow there.
articles.summary: Black Hills cattle losses put at ten per cent because of deep snow.

articles.text: Authentic reports from Montana seem to indicate that the calf crop will average higher in most districts there than in the Bad Lands districts of Dakota. That this is the case is owing to no other reason than of an insufficient supply of bulls. From all we can learn, however, this will be remedied in the future as an abundance of bulls will be put on the range.
articles.summary: Montana's calf crop expected to beat the Bad Lands' because of the local shortage of bulls.

articles.text: An exchange says; "A correspondent wishes to know whether the Illinois State Board of Agriculture will, at their annual fair this year, permit the exhibition of cattle, and also if the St. Louis Fair Association will do the same or rule them out entirely, as they did last year?" We think that under the present quarantine regulations, no cattle will be admitted unless accompanied by a clean bill of health.
articles.summary: Comment on whether cattle will be exhibited at the Illinois and St. Louis fairs under quarantine rules.

articles.text: Messrs. Fisher and Deffebach, who have just returned from the E6 say that the report of the death of nearly all the short-horn bulls driven there last summer, is false. There are about five hundred bulls at the E6 bull-camp, and of these only about twenty have died, really a very light loss for bulls. The grass is so abundant in the neighborhood that the E6 outfit will put up about five hundred tons this summer.
articles.summary: Fisher and Deffebach report only about twenty of five hundred bulls at the E6 bull-camp died; the outfit will put up five hundred tons of hay.

articles.text: The abundance of rain this spring has forced the grass wonderfully. In fact it has grown a little too fast and although twice as abundant, is not as strengthening as it was last year, judging by the condition of cattle. This will soon be remedied and quality and quantity will rule together. Old timers say that the only year they remember when grass was so abundant was that of 1882. Last year it was a matter of great difficulty to get hay in sufficient quantities. This year there is plenty everywhere.
articles.summary: Spring rains have produced the most abundant grass since 1882.

articles.text: The Las Animas, Col., stockgrowers, association met not long ago in Trinidad and passed resolutions which meant war to the knife against any man who attempted to cross the ranges of any members of the association, with southern cattle. The northern Colorado men are in favor of a trail but Las Animas and Bent counties are strongly opposed to the plan. Several large herds are now on the southern border of Colorado in one of Joe Pennell's "jack pots." At present they cannot cross Colorado and even if they could, would surely be stopped at Wyoming, as the authorities there are determined not to let any cattle in that have not passed the ninety days in quarantine.
articles.summary: Las Animas, Colo., stockgrowers vow to stop southern cattle crossing their ranges.

articles.text: The loss on cattle in the Hills country has been greatly exaggerated except on late through cattle. In this class the loss in several instances has gone above twenty-five per cent. The loss on wintered cattle has not reached five per cent. however, in any case and good judges estimate ten per cent. on all classes as high. Out of a bunch of two hundred and fifty in Cave Hills, John Arrington's herd, all but four have been rounded up. These four are as likely to be strayed as dead. The upper Little Missouri and Belle Fourche round-ups are finished and all the cowmen are greatly pleased at the smallness of the loss, contrary to their expectations, and the largeness of the calf crop.
articles.summary: Hills-country cattle losses exaggerated; upper Little Missouri and Belle Fourche round-ups finished with small losses and a large calf crop.

articles.text: A car of very fine short-horn bulls from Ontario was received by J. L. Truscott last Friday.
articles.summary: J. L. Truscott received a carload of short-horn bulls from Ontario.

articles.text: It has been found that in many diseases of horse and cattle, vaccination is a radical cure. It has been found so in black-leg and would doubtless prove equally effectual in other diseases.
articles.summary: Note on vaccination against black-leg and other stock diseases.

articles.text: Lieut. J. M. T. Partello, of Ft. Keogh, is one of the best and most entertaining writers on stock interests that there is now in the west. He is a very prolific writer and none of his articles contain the twaddle and highly colored accounts of profits so common to most writer on stock not directly interested in the cattle business.
articles.summary: Praise for Lieut. J. M. T. Partello of Ft. Keogh as a writer on stock interests.

articles.text:
At Medora of course the cowboy was in great force, and the ladies of the party one and all fell in love with him; not with any one individual cowboy, but with the general class. There were not enough cowboys to go round all the ladies, so each one stood the center of an admiring party (husbands being away in the background, to whom he distributed cartridges and tabs of fringe from his pantaloons as souvenirs. The conductor's lady-killing capacities are proverbial, but when he comes in competition with the untamed cowboy he finds himself side-tracked with some rapidity. The ticket-punch stands no show with a Smith & Wesson 44. When the slaughter-house inspection was over the cowboys gave an extempore exhibition of lariat practice, which was well worth seeing. They lariated cows and ponies, they lariated dogs, they lariated each other, they lariated the ladies' hearts and carried them away hanging from the "fraid straps" of their saddles. In fact the air of Medora was full of whirling lariats until the train moved out, and for every lariat in the air there were half a dozen handkerchiefs waving from the windows of the cars.—[Minneapolis Tribune.

Levi's "mash" is responsible for the above. We are at a loss to tell to what further heights her imagination would have reached if her ink had held out.
articles.summary: Reprint of a Minneapolis Tribune account of an excursion party's stop at Medora, with cowboys giving a lariat exhibition after the slaughter-house inspection, plus the Cow Boy's teasing comment.

articles.headline: THE LOST CABIN GOLD MINES. By J. S. Warn.
articles.text:
I obtained permission of Captain Hulburt to take a party up in the mountains to prospect. Fourteen of us made preparations, took six days provisions and pulled out to the Big Horn mountains. The train was to travel on, making as much speed as possible and when we had finished prospecting we were to come down and overtake it. Instead of six days, our prospecting tour took twenty. Travelling up the west side of the snowy range we prospected along wherever there seemed any signs of gold. We found very little to reward our search and before the six days were up, we were ready to join the train. This we found a difficult task as it was impossible to get over the range of snow. After repeated failures we were forced to take the back track. Finally we found a pass through the range and came out on the east side all right. Here we found nothing except snow, rocks, creeks, lakes and an abundance of all kinds of game, but no gold, although if it had been a foot thick on the ground, we wouldn't have seen it. Getting down off the mountains we struck the wagon trail and pulled out for the train as fast as we could go and there might have been ten thousands cabins near us for all the attention we paid to anything but the trail. We froze to it like the gold fever to an old prospector. We finally came up to the train camped on the Little Big Horn river, waiting for us. Our reception was very cordial for after the threats made by the Indians and our lengthened absence, two weeks longer than we expected, the people in the train had about given up hope of ever seeing us again.

While the train was in camp, prospectors had been sent out everywhere on the east side of the mountains, but they had found no cabin or trace of one.

In the meantime, Bozeman's train had come on and passed us, intending to wait for us at the Big Horn river. When we reached Captain Hulbert's camp on the Little Big Horn, everything was in an uproar. There had been so many failures to find even a clue of the lost cabin, that it finally began to be believed that Hulbert had been misleading the train. These suspicions rapidly grew into complaints, these culminating in threats and when we arrived it seemed as though every man in camp could only be satisfied by Hulbert's death. Everyone was fairly crazy with disappointment and their rage was about to be expended on Captain Hulbert. From suspicions and complaints all were now saying that Hulbert had lied to them and led them off on a wild goose chase for some purpose of his own. Every preparation had been made to hang the Captain and it was altogether the worst crowd I ever saw. The Captain hadn't a friend in camp. He sat to one side, his head down in his hands, his elbows on his knees, staring vacantly at the ground. His heart was broken. I never saw a man in a more pitiable state and I made up my mind that I would be his friend at any rate. I went up to him and called him by name. He raised up, grabbed me by the hand and fairly cried for joy that we had arrived in time to save him. He said that he had found he was in the wrong range of mountains, a mistake easily made as he had travelled away from them during the night. It was impossible to make the crowd believe anything and I didn't try much. I jumped on a wagon tongue and talked about five minutes and finally dared the first man to come with a rope. No one came.

(Continued.)
articles.summary: Installment of J. S. Warn's reminiscence of the Lost Cabin gold-mine expedition: prospecting in the Big Horn mountains and saving Captain Hulbert from a lynch mob.

articles.text: The telephone line is proving of great convenience.
articles.summary: The telephone line is proving convenient.

articles.text: There is not a cleaner town on the road than Medora.
articles.summary: Medora called the cleanest town on the road.

articles.text: The skating rink will only open Saturday evenings hereafter.
articles.summary: The skating rink will open only on Saturday evenings.

articles.text: A Howe platform scales has been placed in front of the Co's. offices.
articles.summary: Howe platform scales installed in front of the company's offices.

articles.text: Ed. Severson has nearly recovered from his wound and is already out of bed.
articles.summary: Ed. Severson nearly recovered from his wound.

articles.text: Bert. Zigler is in St. Paul. He will return here some time during the summer.
articles.summary: Bert. Zigler in St. Paul, to return during the summer.

articles.text: The new refrigerator cars are of the Hamilton patent and are giving perfect satisfaction.
articles.summary: The new Hamilton-patent refrigerator cars give satisfaction.

articles.text: John O'Sullivan has located at Butte City, where his tonsorial shingle will fly in the breeze.
articles.summary: John O'Sullivan has set up as a barber in Butte City.

articles.text: Don't forget the meeting to-morrow night to arrange for field-day sports on the fourth of July.
articles.summary: Reminder of tomorrow night's meeting to plan Fourth of July field-day sports.

articles.text: E. G. Paddock's new building, to be occupied by the Boston clothing house is nearing completion.
articles.summary: E. G. Paddock's new building for the Boston clothing house is nearly done.

articles.text: The cooler of the old slaughter-house is rapidly beieg transformed into one equal in all respects to the new coolers.
articles.summary: The old slaughter-house cooler is being rebuilt to match the new coolers.

articles.text: Dick Carr was kicked yesterday by one of his babies, commonly called mules, and is taking an enforced lay-off of a few days.
articles.summary: Dick Carr was kicked by a mule yesterday.

articles.text: William Tolbert is conducting the Elk in first-class style and would be pleased to see his friends at all times. Give him a call.
articles.summary: William Tolbert is running the Elk.

articles.text: M. W. McDonald has bought out John Warn's resturant and will run it up to the highest "Oyster Grotto" style of excellence.
articles.summary: M. W. McDonald bought John Warn's restaurant.

articles.text: Frank Axthelm, of Miles City, is taking Fred Banan's place as barber, while the latter completes his term of service at Ft. Keogh.
articles.summary: Frank Axthelm of Miles City replaces barber Fred Banan, who is finishing his service at Ft. Keogh.

articles.text: Joe Ferris expects to be established in business on this side the river inside of six weeks. Mr. Ellison is now assisting him in the store.
articles.summary: Joe Ferris expects to move his business to this side of the river within six weeks.

articles.text: Almost every train from the east leaves one or more tourists at Medora, who are intent on looking at the beautiful scenery of the Bad Lands.
articles.summary: Tourists arrive on almost every eastern train to see the Bad Lands.

articles.text: Miss Taylor, of Boston, a young friend of Mr. and Mrs. Wade came last Friday evening and will spend the summer at the Tepee bottom ranch.
articles.summary: Miss Taylor of Boston arrived to spend the summer at the Wades' Tepee bottom ranch.

articles.text: Al. Gifford came down from Glendive yesterday. He has been thinking of going to South America but should this fail he intends to settle in Medora.
articles.summary: Al. Gifford came from Glendive and may settle in Medora.

articles.text: W. H. Holland, of Buffalo, Wyoming, sold fifty herd of fine steers on Monday to the Co. They averaged 1171 pounds and dressed out almost as well as fall cattle. The bunch sold for $4.40.
articles.summary: W. H. Holland of Buffalo, Wyo., sold fifty steers to the company at $4.40.

articles.text: The next lot of cattle from the Hashknife will be delivered July 1. Full time at the slaughter-house may begin then. It is more likely to be a week later.
articles.summary: Next Hashknife cattle due July 1; full-time slaughtering may begin then.

articles.text: Mrs. M. M. Coleman was prostrated last Saturday by a kind of spasm that left her entirely unconscious for several days. She is now considered out of danger.
articles.summary: Mrs. M. M. Coleman was stricken by a spasm but is out of danger.

articles.text: There are constant expressions of satisfaction and delight at the able manner in which Arch. Boyd and wife conduct the Northern Pacific hotel. It is a credit to Medora.
articles.summary: Praise for Arch. Boyd and wife's management of the Northern Pacific hotel.

articles.text: Medora has never looked prettier than at present. A walk to the top of the neighboring buttes will be well rewarded by the magnificent view at the feet of the spectator.
articles.summary: Medora has never looked prettier.

articles.text: Our thanks are due in this public manner to the able and entirely satisfactory way in which J. C. Fisher and Levi Deffebach have conducted the Cow Boy during our absence.
articles.summary: Packard thanks J. C. Fisher and Levi Deffebach for running the Cow Boy in his absence.

articles.text: T. J. Kerr, whom all in Medora know and like, has his summer home on the banks of White Bear lake. Never have we had a pleasanter time than when entertained there by Mr. Kerr and his charming wife.
articles.summary: Packard was entertained by T. J. Kerr at his White Bear Lake summer home.

articles.text: The condition of the cattle is not at all satisfactory for killing and the Co. will shut down until July 1st. Between fifty and a hundred head a day will then be killed until the 15th, when work will begin on full time.
articles.summary: The slaughter-house shuts down until July 1 because cattle are not fit for killing.

articles.text: The Marquis, wife and friends and J. N. Simpson will make up a party for a pleasure excursion to the neighborhood of the Big Horn mountains. The party will start about July 15, and will be under the leadership of Vic Smith.
articles.summary: The Marquis de Mores, his wife, friends and J. N. Simpson plan a Big Horn excursion about July 15 led by Vic Smith.

articles.text: J. C. Fisher and Rassie Deffebach started last Friday for the E6 and returned last evening. They report the grass as knee-high all over the Cave Hills district, as good feed as there has ever been in the country. They stopped at Harry Tarbell's and are enthusiastic over his outfit. Everything is arranged in first-class shape and there is every probability of ninety per cent. of foals. Mr. Huidekoper is now visiting at the ranch. At the E6 they found one of the most systematically conducted ranches they ever visited. There are about thirty cow-boys here under the foremanship of Russ Wilson and each one has his duty as well defined as have the employes in a manufactory. Coming back they went to Arrington's ranch in Cave Hills, probably as pretty a location as there is in the country. Here they found Fred Willard and in company they came to Medora, striking the river at Eaton's logging camp and coming down the river road.
articles.summary: J. C. Fisher and Rassie Deffebach report on a trip to the E6, Harry Tarbell's horse ranch and Arrington's ranch in the Cave Hills.

articles.text: Carl Parks formerly of Mandan, is spending the summer here.
articles.summary: Carl Parks of Mandan is summering in Medora.

articles.text: Prof. Wellung's entertainment at the rink on the evening of the 4th.
articles.summary: Prof. Wellung to give an entertainment at the rink on the Fourth.

articles.text: Fred Willard has been appointed stock inspector at Medora and arrived last evening to enter upon his duties. Fred made a host of friends while here and the appointment will give general satisfaction.
articles.summary: Fred Willard appointed stock inspector at Medora, arriving last evening.

articles.text: The queerest malformation in the shape of a deer horn we ever saw is now on exhibition at Bob Robert's saloon. One old horn was not shed and the new horn grew up around it in a very curious manner.
articles.summary: A malformed deer horn is on exhibit at Bob Roberts' saloon.

articles.text: John Warn left Monday for Miles City where he intends organizing a party to go in search of the "Lost Cabin" gold mines. He has the good-will of all on his trip. His continued story will be concluded next week.
articles.summary: John Warn left for Miles City to organize a Lost Cabin gold-mine search party.

articles.text: Mrs. A. Fox, of Minnoiska, Minn., and Mrs. E. Fox, of Ojata, Dak., made a call at the Cow Boy office Monday. Their husbands will be remembered as two of the party who went in a boat from here to Bismarck last May.
articles.summary: Mrs. A. Fox and Mrs. E. Fox called at the Cow Boy office.

articles.text: The base-ball craze has again struck Medora and an unexpected number of good players have already been developed. We understand that Glendive and Dickinson will have a match game on the 4th. If nines are organized at both these places it will be easy to arrange contests with them.
articles.summary: Baseball craze in Medora; Glendive and Dickinson to play on the Fourth.

articles.text: Much to the disappointment of our readers, who have noticed the literary improvement in the Cow Boy under the able leadership of Messrs. Fisher and Deffebach, the editor turned up on the late train Friday evening. The population of Medora is also increased by an editorial better half.
articles.summary: Editor Packard returned Friday evening, bringing his wife.

articles.text: Baron A. von Steiger has had another horse-thief experience. He bought a horse in McLean county and the same night it was stolen from him. He followed the trail for about three weeks and finally got the horse. Taking it back home it was again taken from him by its rightful owner who lived near Ft. Stevenson. A horse is not worth much unless accompanied by a bill of sale signed by a responsible party.
articles.summary: Baron A. von Steiger recovered a stolen horse only to lose it to its rightful owner near Ft. Stevenson.

articles.text: There will be a great fourth of July entertainment and ball combined at the roller rink, the evening of the immortal fourth. The doors will be open at 7:30 and the misery will begin at 8:30. In connection with Prof. Wellung's magic entertainment there will be a variety consisting of double and single song and dance, negro sketches, laughable puns etc., lasting until 10 o'clock, after which dancing will commence and continue until everyone is dead.
articles.summary: A Fourth of July entertainment and ball planned at the roller rink.

articles.text: And now we wish "to arise to remark" that the glorious 4th is almost upon us and no preparations have been made for any celebration during the day. The entertainment at the rink in the evening will doubtless be interesting but besides this, much enjoyment could be had by contests of various kinds during the day. To further this end we will issue a call for a meeting to elect a board to conduct the entertainment. The meeting will be held to-morrow, Friday evening at 8:00 o'clock at the rink. Let everyone turn out.
articles.summary: Call for a meeting Friday evening at the rink to plan daytime Fourth of July contests.

articles.text: A meeting was held Monday evening to organize a church society, to see how many would take an active interest in paying the expenses of holding weekly service here. The officers elected were; J. C. Fisher, President; T. W. Gordon, Vice-president and W. B. Wright, Secretary. It was decided to find out how much could be raised weekly and for this purpose the secretary was instructed to prepare lists both of those who wish to become members of the association and of those who will contribute a stated sum weekly. The meeting then adjourned to meet early next week and hear the report of the secretary.
articles.summary: A church society was organized Monday with J. C. Fisher president.
